Start here

What might your dog be saying?

Tap a moment to get a quick, low-pressure read. Then check the whole body before you act.

A softer read

Loose usually means comfortable.

A relaxed dog can still be alert or excited. Look for easy movement and the ability to choose what happens next.

  • Look forSoft eyes, a wiggly middle, and a mouth that rests open or gently closed.
  • Try thisKeep the moment predictable. Let your dog approach, sniff, or move away.
  • Don’t assumeA wag only tells you the tail is moving—not whether the feeling is happy.
  • Helpful next stepNotice what changed just before the body changed. Context is the missing clue.
Everyday behavior

What dogs do—and what it can tell you.

Behavior is a clue, not a verdict. Look at the whole dog, the moment around it, and what they can choose next.

Information gathering

Sniffing & exploring

Nose work helps dogs learn about the world and can be calming enrichment.

Try: Give sniff walks time instead of rushing every stop.

Notice: Sudden frantic sniffing can also be a way to release pressure.

Communication

Barking & vocalizing

Barks can mean alert, excitement, frustration, fear, or a request for help.

Try: Check distance, trigger, rhythm, and recovery before responding.

Notice: Punishment may silence a warning without changing the feeling.

Enrichment

Chewing & shredding

Chewing is normal exploration and can help a dog settle when the outlet is safe.

Try: Trade unsafe items for an appropriate chew—never chase or grab.

Notice: A sudden increase may point to boredom, stress, or discomfort.

Natural instinct

Digging

Dogs may dig to explore scent, cool down, bury treasure, play, or make an escape route.

Try: Offer a safe digging spot and reward choosing it.

Notice: Digging at doors or fences can signal urgency or a need for more support.

Energy release

Zoomies

Fast loops and sudden sprints are often a normal release of energy or arousal.

Try: Clear hazards and let the run happen in a safe space.

Notice: Afterward, watch whether the body can settle, drink, and rest.

Greeting

Jumping up

Jumping usually comes from excitement, a learned greeting, or wanting access to a person.

Try: Reward four paws on the floor and keep greetings calm and consistent.

Notice: Turning away is clearer and kinder than pushing the dog down.

A request

Pawing & nudging

A paw or nose bump can ask for attention, access, play, food, or reassurance.

Try: Notice what happens next and teach a calmer way to ask.

Notice: A tense face or repeated nudging can mean the dog needs support, not more touch.

Recovery

Resting & hiding

Choosing a bed, quiet corner, or hideaway is a healthy way to recover and regulate.

Try: Protect the rest spot and let your dog come back to you.

Notice: A sudden, persistent change in resting or social behavior deserves a health check.

The whole-body check

Read the sentence, not one word.

Dogs speak in clusters of signals. Scan from face to feet, then add the setting: who is nearby, what just happened, and whether your dog can leave.

  • 01
    EarsForward can mean interest; pinned back can mean worry, appeasement, or simply a breeze.
  • 02
    EyesSoft and blinking is different from a fixed stare or showing the whites.
  • 03
    MouthA loose open mouth is not the same as a tight mouth, lip lick, or repeated yawn.
  • 04
    BodyLoose curves invite connection; freezing or leaning away asks for more space.
  • 05
    TailHeight, speed, and stiffness matter together. A wag is not a universal “yes.”
  • 06
    ChoiceThe clearest clue: can your dog move closer, move away, or take a break?
  • 07
    MovementSpeed, direction, rhythm, and whether the dog can stop all add meaning to the pose.
  • 08
    Situation / contextRead what happened before, who is nearby, and whether the dog has a safe way out.
A kind default

When in doubt, make space.

Distance is information. Give your dog a clear exit, lower the intensity, and notice whether their body softens. If they keep escalating or seem unwell, contact a qualified force-free professional or veterinarian.

1
Pause the pressureStop reaching, hugging, cornering, or asking for more.
2
Open an exitTurn your body sideways and give your dog room to choose.
3
Listen to the changeSoftening means the space helped. If not, add more distance.
WagSignals ✦

Educational guidance, not a diagnosis. Every dog is an individual; breed, health, age, history, and context all matter.
